title: What Unitika actually sells
body:
Unitika today is three companies sharing one balance sheet. The largest — and the one that now defines the company's investment case — makes polymer films and engineering plastics. The second makes glass fabrics thin enough to disappear inside a smartphone's memory module. The third makes textiles, is being systematically dismantled, and contributed ¥50 million of operating profit on ¥23.9 billion of revenue in the nine months to December 2025. Understanding which of these three stories you are buying is the central analytical challenge the company presents.

## Polymers: the cash engine

The Polymers segment generated ¥42.5 billion of revenue in the nine months to December 2025, representing 44% of group sales, and ¥7.5 billion of operating profit — a 67% increase year-on-year and comfortably the largest profit contributor in the group. The segment spans two distinct product families: Films and Plastics.

Films are the older, more established half. Unitika produces nylon and polyester barrier films for food packaging — the invisible infrastructure of Japan's convenience-store and ready-meal supply chain. The flagship product, **EMBLEM-HG**, is a retort barrier film designed for high-temperature sterilisation pouches. Management has cited double-digit volume growth for EMBLEM-HG across the nine-month period, driven by domestic Japanese food manufacturers seeking lighter, more recyclable alternatives to aluminium laminate. The claim is credible; the product competes on performance characteristics (oxygen transmission rate, puncture resistance at elevated temperatures) rather than commodity price, which gives it some insulation from Chinese competition.

The second film growth product is **UniPeel**, a silicone-free polyethylene-terephthalate release film. Conventional PET release films use a silicone coating that creates contamination risks in semiconductor fabrication — silicone deposits on capacitor arrays and substrate surfaces are a known yield killer. UniPeel eliminates the silicone layer through a proprietary surface-treatment process. Semiconductor manufacturers are actively qualifying it for multilayer ceramic capacitor (MLCC) processing and for advanced substrate manufacturing, where ultra-clean peel characteristics matter at nanometre tolerances. Adoption is at an early commercial stage; Unitika has not disclosed volume figures separately, but the segment commentary notes "electronic-materials demand drove industrial film" growth throughout the nine-month period.

Plastics — engineering resins and specialty polymers sold to electric, electronic and automotive customers — rounded out the segment. Automotive demand was described as weak, consistent with the broader Japanese auto sector. Electronics, however, compensated: engineering plastics for motor housings, connectors and consumer-electronics chassis all grew. Specialty polymers, including nylon-based compounds for precision-injection applications, showed steady expansion.

The operating margin for Polymers reached approximately 17.8% in the nine-month period — high for a Japanese materials company of this scale and the clearest evidence that the segment restructuring of recent years removed genuine cost drag.

## Performance Materials: the high-margin frontier

Performance Materials is smaller by revenue — ¥29.1 billion over nine months — but the segment that most clearly signals where Unitika wants to go. Operating profit of ¥1.4 billion represented a 252% year-on-year increase; the prior-year comparison was depressed, but even on an absolute basis the trajectory is sharp.

The segment contains five product lines, and they are not equally interesting.

**Glass Fibers** is the star. Unitika produces ultra-thin Low Coefficient of Thermal Expansion (Low CTE) glass fabrics and ultra-thin E Glass Fabrics for the printed circuit boards used in high-end mobile memory — specifically the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and LPDDR stacks that sit inside flagship smartphones and AI inference chips. These fabrics run at thicknesses below 15 microns; the Low CTE specification controls the dimensional change of the substrate during thermal cycling, which matters acutely when you are stacking seven or eight dies and expecting sub-micron registration. Management commentary described electronic-material glass fabrics as growing "significantly" in the period, consistent with the HBM supply build that dominated the semiconductor supply chain through 2025. Industrial glass fabrics — for tents, architectural membranes, composite sheets — were described as "robust," which in Unitika's cautious disclosure register generally means flat to moderately up.

**Activated Carbon Fibers** address two orthogonal markets. The water-purification application — hollow-fibre membranes and activated-carbon filter cartridges — has been described as Unitika's mainstay in this product line, with strong domestic demand. The VOC-removal application (solvent-recovery sheets for industrial air exhaust) had been weak through prior periods but showed overseas recovery in the nine months to December. Neither application is particularly high-margin; the business competes on material performance and long-standing customer qualification rather than price leadership.

**Non-Woven Fabrics** deserves a specific note because its shape is changing. The spunbond product — polypropylene non-wovens used in crop-protection agriculture and automotive interior lining — was strong. The spunlace cotton product, however, is no longer fully Unitika's. Zuiko Corporation, a Japanese converting-machinery manufacturer, acquired the spunlace cotton non-wovens business (marketed under the COTEX brand) in 2025. What remains in the segment is the industrial-facing portion; the consumer-hygiene-adjacent revenue has departed. Unitika is still seeking a buyer for TUSCO, its Thailand-based polyester spunbond operation, as of October 2025 — a loose end that adds modest uncertainty to the segment's forward cost structure.

**Glass Beads** and **Industrial Fibers** are steady but not strategic. Glass beads for road-marking retro-reflectivity face intensifying price pressure from Chinese manufacturers. High-strength polyester yarns within industrial fibers — used in geotextiles and reinforcing applications — are growing, but from a small base.

## Fibers & Textiles: controlled demolition

The Fibers & Textiles segment recorded ¥23.9 billion of revenue in the nine months to December 2025, essentially flat year-on-year (+0.8%), and ¥50 million of operating profit. That last number is actually an achievement: the comparable period in the prior year produced a ¥560 million operating loss. The segment has been loss-making for long enough that a breakeven is read as stabilisation, not success.

The commercial logic behind the segment's continued existence is simple: the businesses take time to transfer or close, and premature shutdown destroys more value than a managed exit. Seiren Co., Ltd. is acquiring the textile business at the Okazaki Plant in a transaction structured as a share acquisition in a newly formed company split jointly from Unitika and Nippon Ester. Shikibo Ltd. is taking part of the apparel-related fibre business. Within what remains, public-sector uniforms — police, municipal workers, railway staff — provide steady low-margin volume. General apparel is weak. Overseas denim, primarily from operations in Southeast Asia, is described as solid. Civil-engineering applications and household-product industrial materials are the small bright spots.

The Other segment — ¥71 million of revenue, ¥28 million operating loss — is a rounding error in the consolidated accounts. The filing does not provide granular disclosure on its contents; at this scale, the segment is almost certainly a catch-all for legacy service entities or IP-licensing income that does not fit cleanly elsewhere.

## The forward bet

The DIC Corporation partnership, announced at CES in December 2025, offers the clearest forward indicator of where Unitika's specialty pivot is aimed. The two companies are co-developing a polyphenylene sulfide (PPS) film for millimetre-wave printed circuit boards — the substrate layer inside 5G and automotive radar systems that must maintain dielectric properties at frequencies above 24 GHz. PPS film at mmWave specifications is a difficult material problem; conventional laminates introduce signal loss that degrades radar range and accuracy. Unitika brings the film-extrusion capability; DIC brings chemical formulation expertise and customer relationships in the PCB supply chain.

No revenue has been attributed to this programme, and it would be premature to model it. What the partnership confirms is a deliberate move toward applications — semiconductor substrates, advanced PCBs, precision release films — where material performance rather than volume determines pricing power. Whether the balance sheet, now stabilised by the REVIC capital injection but still carrying a 25.2% equity ratio, can sustain the development investment that transition requires is the question the next chapter must address.
